ld.name: Lupaia in Torrita di Siena
ld.description: We’ve all seen more than a few hotels that could fairly be described as “Tuscan rustic,” but Lupaia makes most of them look like half-measures. Here the farmhouse charm is cranked up to eleven or twelve, especially in its open kitchen, where a daily four-course dinner is made out of produce from the hotel’s own organic garden. And it’s in plentiful supply in the rooms as well, carefully adapted from five painstakingly renovated historical structures, each of which is an architectural mosaic of Tuscan styles, with contemporary comforts under centuries-old roof beams and rough-hewn textures alongside finely wrought furnishings.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Santa Caterina in Amalfi
ld.description: It’s the rare traditional-style hotel that really gets hearts racing, but the Santa Caterina is an absolute classic. Family-owned for the better part of a century, it sits high on a hillside facing the sea — guests ride an elevator down to the hotel’s private beach club, for the ultimate storybook Italian-coast experience.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Il Sereno in Torno
ld.description: There’s plenty of neoclassical bling on the shores of Lake Como. And historic villas, too, though these days, the centuries-old architecture is outnumbered by extravagant imitations. Thankfully the team behind the brand-new Il Sereno, located just outside the village of Torno on the lake’s eastern shore, is taking things in a bold new direction.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are welcome in the hotel with a housekeeping fee of 250 euros per stay, to a maximum of one pet and less than 12kgs. Pets must be supervised at all times and must be on a leash in public places.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Casa Angelina in Praiano
ld.description: Praiano isn’t the most famous town on the Amalfi Coast, but its appeal is undeniable: it’s just beyond Positano, which not only places it outside the most crowded stretch of the coast, but gives it an astonishing view of Positano itself, along with the dramatic seascapes to the west. This is where you’ll find Casa Angelina, a rare hotel that makes a virtue of modern architecture and design even in these most traditional environs — and, in the process, establishes a tone of understated luxury that few hotels anywhere can match.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Il San Pietro di Positano in Positano
ld.description: Even by Italian standards, Positano is naturally breathtaking: its colorful houses and churches cling desperately to the mountainside, with postcard-perfect views of the sea coming seemingly a dime a dozen. Perhaps a bit more than a dime, actually; it’s possible (if unlikely) that there are still some secret places left on the Italian coasts, untouched by tourism, but even if that’s true, Positano certainly isn’t one of them.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed but are restricted from common areas such as the beach club and restaurants.

award.awardFor: Three MICHELIN Keys · An extraordinary stay

ld.name: Villa Fiorella Art Hotel in Massa Lubrense
ld.description: Massa Lubrense is perhaps best known as a stop on the way to the Amalfi Coast, or a place to catch a boat across the Gulf of Naples to the island of Capri. But it’s a worthy destination in its own right. It’s here, according to Greek legend, that sirens first lured sailors to crash into the rocky shore. Looking down at the coastline from Art Hotel Villa Fiorella, a quiet boutique hotel set in an olive grove high over the water, it’s easy to believe in the myth.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: COMO Castello del Nero in Barberino Tavarnelle
ld.description: Surrounded by world-famous vineyards and within easy day-trip distance of both Florence and Siena, the Chianti region of Tuscany is hardly suffering from a shortage of worthwhile attractions. But COMO Castello Del Nero takes the concept of stately country retreat a step further than various other villas and resorts in the area, offering a full-service COMO Shambhala Retreat spa designed to help guests unwind after pounding the city pavement on church and art tours — or perhaps to detox after one too many wine tastings.
ld.petsAllowed: \n Small Pets are allowed (max 10 kg)

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Il Borro in San Giustino Valdarno
ld.description: For some of us, the fantasy of owning a Tuscan villa is sufficiently romantic; if you’re more ambitious, however, you set your sights on something closer to an old-fashioned Tuscan principality. Enter Il Borro, the sprawling estate in San Giustino Valdarno that Ferruccio Ferragamo bought in 1993 and have since been developing into the Tuscan luxury hotel to end them all. Il Borro comprises no less than an acclaimed, hundred-plus acre vineyard and winery, vast groves of olive trees amidst the cypress and oaks, plenty of rolling green hills, three villas, another three lavish farmhouses and — here’s the real coup de grâce — an entire restored medieval village. Given the scope of the estate, it’s almost unnecessary to mention that it also contains tennis courts, a driving range and a football pitch, to name just the athletic facilities.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed on request and free of charge.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Hotel Vilòn in Rome
ld.description: Like many of Rome’s finest boutique hotels, Hotel Vilòn aims to provide not just luxury-hotel service and comfort, but residential charm and intimacy as well. The setting, in the city’s historic center, in a 16th-century house annexed to the Palazzo Borghese, is as romantic as it gets, and close by to many of the familiar attractions. But not for a moment does it feel like a busy city-center hotel; once inside, the quiet is practically monastic.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Hotel Capo La Gala in Vico Equense
ld.description: In the mad rush from Naples to Capri or the far side of the Sorrentine Peninsula it’s too easy to breeze right past Sorrento itself; a shame, for while not technically on the Amalfi Coast this side of the Bay of Naples is blessed with some extraordinary spots, the village of Vico Equense among them. It scarcely gets more picturesque than this gorgeously weathered seaside village, though the Hotel Capo La Gala, just on its fringes, gives it a run for its money.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Country House Villadorata in Noto
ld.description: Nestled in the heart of the Val di Noto — a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the cradle of Sicilian Baroque — Country House Villadorata, the countryside counterpart to Seven Rooms in Noto, is the result of the restoration of a late 19th-century rural estate. Today, it stands as an elegant eco-resort surrounded by 57 acres of countryside, cultivated in harmony with the principles of biodynamic agriculture.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Grand Hotel Excelsior Vittoria in Sorrento
ld.description: The Grand Hotel Excelsior Vittoria benefits from a phenomenal location, right in the heart of Sorrento, high on a cliff overlooking the harbor and separated from the bustling Piazza Tasso by orange groves and acres of parkland. The hotel itself comprises three separate villas, all built between 1834 and 1880. This is a true Grand Hotel in the old style, its past guests including Wagner and Goethe, and the opera singer Enrico Caruso was a resident for a time in the twenties, his suite today remaining more or less as he left it.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Punta Tragara in Capri
ld.description: It’s humbling, if you’re from somewhere other than Italy, to think about how naturally blessed the peninsula and its islands have been. And they haven’t exactly let all that natural beauty go to waste either. Seemingly everywhere you look is another hidden gem, another one-of-a-kind hotel. Take, for example, the Hotel Punta Tragara, on the island of Capri.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Aman Venice in Venice
ld.description: Your eyes do not deceive you: the Aman Venice is exactly what the name implies. It’s fitting that Aman, those masters of luxe villas on jade-green desert islands, would choose this as the setting for their first city hotel. Like many of Aman’s far-flung, impossibly photogenic locales, there’s a sense that Venice isn’t quite of this earth. And, more prosaically, they’ve already perfected the craft of the waterborne arrival on those selfsame desert islands, and it’s a skill that transfers seamlessly to Venice’s canals.

award.awardFor: Three MICHELIN Keys · An extraordinary stay

ld.name: Castel Fragsburg in Merano
ld.description: Castel Fragsburg occupies what may be the most privileged position in this spectacularly beautiful corner of South Tyrol, Italy’s famous patch of Alpine-style paradise. It’s located inside an elegant hunting lodge that first opened its doors nearly four centuries ago — and on a nearby cliffside is the 14th-century castle for which it was built. (The castle now serves as a thoroughly unique events venue for hotel guests.) You’ll spot its red gables from afar as you navigate the hairpin roads leading up from the ancient spa town of Merano; you’ll know you’ve arrived when you see a antique motorbike, complete with a sidecar, parked outside.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Byblos Art Hotel Villa Amistà in San Pietro in Cariano
ld.description: We’ve seen design hotels, and we’ve seen fashion hotels, but the Byblos Art Hotel Villa Amistà is more than this: it’s also something like a museum, a showcase for a family’s impressive collection of 20th-century design objects and contemporary artworks, right down to the gallery-style placards in every room listing the pieces contained within.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Hotel Lungarno  in Florence
ld.description: When the Ferragamo family moved into the boutique-hotel business, eyebrows were raised — but since then, they’ve proved many times over that they’re just as skilled with a luxury suite as they are with a calfskin lace-up. They’ve got some high-caliber help, of course, in the person of Michele Bönan, Florentine hotel architect extraordinaire. And for this bunch, the Hotel Lungarno is simply another perfectly confident step. Boutique hotels don’t get much more upscale than this, luxury hotels don’t get much more stylish, and the location, right on the south bank of the Arno, is just about beyond compare.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Therasia Resort Sea & Spa in Vulcano
ld.description: You don’t have to be a geologist to guess what kind of island Vulcano is. Black sand, rocky shores, and dramatic landscapes characterize this Aeolian island, just off the northern coast of Sicily. And on its northern edge is Therasia Resort Sea and Spa, from whose cascading salt-water infinity pools you’ll gaze across a narrow strait at the next island, Lipari, less than a mile away.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Botania Relais & Spa in Island of Ischia
ld.description: When it comes to islands in the Bay of Naples, the mind naturally leaps straight to Capri. But around the other end of the bay is the larger, if less storied, island of Ischia. It may lack some of the drama of Capri, and its hotel scene as a whole might not scale the same opulent heights, but it’s possessed of a wilder sort of beauty — and, as you may have guessed by now, some impressive hotels of its own. Among them is Botania Relais & Spa, a tranquil escape tucked away, in classic Ischian style, within a lush two-acre garden estate.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Terra - The Magic Place in Sarentino
ld.description: It makes an extravagant promise, but Terra - The Magic Place lives up to its name. It starts with the location, high in the Italian Dolomites, where the word “magic” is scarcely an exaggeration. The hotel, too, is memorable, a modernist interpretation of Tyrolean chalet architecture. And of course there’s the restaurant that inspired it all: the two-MICHELIN-Star Terra, where chef Heinrich Schneider and his team prepare a one-of-a-kind experience for dinner guests surrounded by breathtaking mountain views — and accompanied by a bottle of wine you’ll personally choose from the cellar.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed on request for an additional fee.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Grand Hotel Principe di Piemonte in Viareggio
ld.description: Apparently the prince prefers the coast. Though the hotel is called the Grand Hotel Principe di Piemonte, it stands on the central promenade in the picturesque town of Viareggio, on the coast of northern Tuscany. One glance at the building and you know what the place is about, its ornate 1920s façade rising in all its splendor above Viareggio’s long sandy beach and the Tyrrhenian Sea just beyond. In short, it’s a classic European resort-hotel in a classic European resort-town.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: La Foresteria Planeta Estate in Menfi
ld.description: Sicily’s Planeta family is perhaps best known for the wines and olive oils that they produce in a multitude of locations all across the island, but with La Foresteria Planeta Estate they turn their hand to hospitality. Here, in the remote far west of Sicily, not far from the town of Menfi, they’ve created a small-scale country retreat, overlooking the vineyards and olive groves of one of this island’s most gently scenic regions.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Hassler Roma in Rome
ld.description: Right at the top of the Spanish Steps, in what has to be one of the most prominent locations in town, is the Hassler Roma, a longtime local institution owned and operated by the same Swiss family since 1893. This fact accounts for two of the Hassler’s strengths, which are rarely found under the same roof: its exceedingly warm welcome and its thoroughly professional manner of operation. And though it’s got as rich a history as any century-old luxury hotel, and remains traditional in its elegance, it’s been kept beautifully up to date.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are not allowed.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Goldene Rose Karthaus in Schnals
ld.description: A corner of Italy where German is spoken, and impossibly jagged mountain peaks rise in the near distance? The Dolomites seem too extraordinary to be true, but the South Tyrolean village of Certosa is a real place, and the family-owned Golden Rose is a beautiful introduction: from the outside, an immaculately well-kept Tyrolean inn, and on the inside, a hotel that’s clearly absorbed the influence of a generation or two of stylish Italian hospitality design.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Reschio Hotel in Lisciano Niccone
ld.description: Italian hoteliers in general are no strangers to working with heritage buildings, but the Castello di Reschio is an extreme example. Set on a vast estate in the picturesque hills of Umbria, near the border with Tuscany, the castle dates back all the way to the tenth century, which makes the decade-plus its owners, an architect and an artist, spent on careful restoration seem like the blink of an eye by comparison.

award.awardFor: Three MICHELIN Keys · An extraordinary stay

ld.name: Riva Lofts Florence in Florence
ld.description: In Italy even the most modern hotel has hundreds or thousands of years of architectural history to deal with; one hypermodern hotel in Rome has a working archaeological site in the basement. By these standards, Riva Lofts is on the young side: this 19th-century complex on the banks of the Arno river has lived only three previous lives — a factory, artisans’ workshops, an architectural studio — on the way to its present incarnation, an immaculately designed ten-suite modernist luxury boutique.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are welcome if well behaved, at 12€ per night, they cannot be left alone in the rooms.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: La Minervetta in Sorrento
ld.description: Contemporary design on the Amalfi coast — that alone makes La Minervetta worth noting. And we’re not using “contemporary” as a euphemism for that faceless minimal international style, either; you’ll find little in the way of greys or cream tones in La Minervetta’s twelve guest rooms.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Susafa in Polizzi Generosa
ld.description: A working farm in Sicily’s rustic, hilly interior, this country boutique hotel distills centuries of hospitality and husbandry into a charming, restful bullseye — it’s commanded the verdant countryside for five generations under the stewardship of the Saeli-Rizzuto family.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Il Palazzo Experimental in Venice
ld.description: The Experimental Group has blossomed quickly from a word-of-mouth Parisian cocktail phenomenon to a full-fledged hospitality concern, with hotels in Paris, London, the Alps, and now Venice — and if there ever were a city whose hotel scene needed an infusion of youthful cool, it’s this one, whose bridges and canals are so thick with tourists you could be forgiven for wondering if there’s any nightlife culture here at all. That’s where Il Palazzo Experimental comes in, of course — not only does its bar, the Experimental Cocktail Club, answer that question in the affirmative, but as a hotel it turns the classic gestures of Venetian design into something fresh, contemporary, even sexy.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Hotel Metropole Venice in Venice
ld.description: Even by Venetian standards, the Hotel Metropole is steeped in history — this was once an orphanage where Vivaldi gave music lessons. More recently, though still decades ago, it was acquired by the Beggiato family, and remains a family-owned and -operated hotel, decorated with the owners’ collections of art and antiques. And while it’s been renovated to keep pace with the times, its style is eclectic and deeply rooted, spanning multiple centuries and incorporating influences from historical Venice to the Far East.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Corte della Maestà in Civita di Bagnoregio
ld.description: All roads may lead to Rome, but there’s no one to stop you from pulling a U-turn. You won’t have to travel far outside the capital before the medieval village of Civita di Bagnoregio rises up into view on a hilltop before you. It’s a vision so magnificent that you’ll have a hard time believing that Italians once nicknamed the place “la cittá che muore” – the dying city. But natural disasters happen even in a landscape as bucolic as this one: an earthquake struck in 1685, and the residents fled, including the bishop, who abandoned his home and seminary.

award.awardFor: Three MICHELIN Keys · An extraordinary stay

ld.name: The Place Firenze  in Florence
ld.description: For just about as long as the phrase “luxury boutique hotel” has been in the travel-industry lexicon, it’s been represented in Florence by The Place Firenze. And while this ultra-chic townhouse on the Piazza di Santa Maria Novella has evolved with the times — architect Luigi Fragola oversaw its most recent renovation — it’s lost none of its appeal. To go from the bustling streets of Florence to a hotel so intimate it lacks even a traditional reception desk is refreshing, to say the least — and while its rooms and suites are as plush and well-equipped as anything in town, they’re so unique and so full of Florentine character that you’ll feel more like a local than a luxury-hotel guest.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Sextantio Le Grotte della Civita in Matera
ld.description: The phrase albergo diffuso might not yet be entirely familiar to English-speaking travelers — or, for that matter, to Italian ones — but the concept that it denotes is one we imagine will quickly catch on. Call it a “distributed hotel” if that makes it clearer — or just take Sextantio Le Grotte della Civita as an example.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Palazzo Albricci Peregrini in Como
ld.description: It’s no secret that some of the most extravagant hotels in the world line the shores of Lake Como itself, but in the town of Como it’s possible to hide away in a hotel that’s a little less conspicuous. And while the Palazzo Albricci Peregrini is an exceedingly private place, tucked safely away from prying eyes, the experience it offers is no less extraordinary than that of its more ostentatious neighbors.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Grand Hotel Minerva  in Florence
ld.description: Florence isn’t exactly short on impressive hotels, but the Grand Hotel Minerva stands out in a few categories. First there’s the location, on the Piazza Santa Maria Novella, right between the rail station and the historic city center. Second, there’s the rooftop pool, a rarity in this town, and a welcome one at that. And third, there’s, well, the whole thing — the hotel originally dates back to the 19th century, but it was famously redesigned in the Fifties by architect Carlo Scarpa, and a more recent renovation at the hands of Piera Tempesti Benelli leaves the Minerva’s particular blend of classical grandeur and mid-century glamour looking as fresh as can be.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets up to 10 kg. /22 are allowed at Grand Hotel Minerva with an additional fee of 30€ per stay. Only one pet per room is admitted. Pets are not allowed in any food & beverage outlets, fitness and wellness area, and the rooftop terrace and pool. Please contact the hotel to know the full pet policy.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Castel Monastero in Castelnuovo Berardenga
ld.description: Castel Monastero began life as an eleventh-century village. Then it became a monastery, complete with an incredible Chianti cellar. Now, roughly a thousand years later, it still sits magisterially on a hill, a high-end luxury hotel, one placed close to Siena, far from most everywhere else, and absolutely worth a detour.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Brunelleschi Hotel in Florence
ld.description: There’s no question the Brunelleschi Hotel has a legitimate claim to the name. With its top-floor view taking in the entire panorama of Brunelleschi’s masterpiece, the Florence Cathedral, it’s more or less as close as you can get to the Duomo without taking religious orders. The location has always been a strength, and after a very thorough renovation, the Brunelleschi can finally boast of interiors that are worthy of the view.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Castello di Vicarello in Cinigiano
ld.description: It’s a testament to what’s special about Tuscany that it’s still even possible to find a part of it that’s not saturated with tourism. Perched on a hilltop surrounded by gently rolling hills, the Castello di Vicarello is one of these places — an authentic 12th-century castle, converted into a charming country house boutique by owners Carlo and Aurora Baccheschi Berti, who moved down from Milan in search of the quiet life.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Sextantio in Santo Stefano di Sessanio
ld.description: To give it its full name, it’s Sextantio Albergo Diffuso; roughly speaking, the Sextantio Distributed Hotel. Which sounds a bit futuristic in English, but is in fact nothing of the sort — it’s a sixteenth-century village, the Abbruzzese mountain village of Santo Stefano di Sessanio, complete with villagers as residents, and packed in between them, distributed amongst the various houses and buildings of the village, are some 29 hotel rooms.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Dimora delle Balze in Noto
ld.description: Sometimes it seems there’s hardly a square kilometer of Italy that doesn’t contain some unmissable sight or some unforgettable hotel. On the eastern side of Sicily, a half-hour inland from Syracuse, and even closer to the beautiful baroque town of Noto, is one of both: a masseria — an old farming estate — whose stone buildings and courtyards have been transformed into a contemporary boutique hotel called Dimora delle Balze.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Locanda Rossa in Capalbio
ld.description: The Maremma, the coastal region where Tuscany meets Lazio, is a bit of a Johnny-come-lately as a holiday destination, though you’d never know it from looking at it today — here a once-impoverished agricultural region has been transformed into, well, a not-at-all-impoverished agricultural region, and one that’s as well known for tourism as for produce. And this fame is due in no small part to a wealth of independent hotels, places like Capalbio’s Locanda Rossa.
ld.petsAllowed: \n Pet-friendly accommodations are available in select room categories with a garden. Please contact customer service prior to arrival for arrangements.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

pages.h1: Villa le Prata - Residenza del Vescovo

ld.name: Villa le Prata - Residenza del Vescovo in Montalcino
ld.description: Every corner of Tuscany has its partisans, surely, but there’s no place quite like Montalcino, famous for the walled hilltop city, its idyllic surroundings, and the region’s coveted Sangiovese Grosso wines. And to that list of attractions you can add at least one extraordinary place to stay. Villa le Prata - Residenza del Vescovo is a scant five minutes’ drive from the city walls, and it’s as pure an introduction to the delights of Tuscan countryside living as you could possibly ask for.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Villa Fontelunga in Foiano della Chiana
ld.description: Villa Fontelunga is not at all the stereotypical Tuscan experience. This Padronale residence has been thoroughly redesigned, and is a charming blend of old and new, an sharp contrast to the wax-museum standard of frescoes-and-antiques Italian villa hotels.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Nordelaia in Cremolino
ld.description: It’s hard to imagine a hospitality experience much more delicious than a farmhouse hotel in the hills of Piedmont. Nordelaia begins with an 800-year-old farmhouse, extensively reimagined by the London-based design studio These White Walls; the result is still beautifully rustic but now also unmistakably modern, full of historical details interwoven with modern fixtures and furnishings.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Palazzo Daniele in Gagliano del Capo
ld.description: There’s no greater cliché in travel writing than “land of contrasts,” but it’s a description that’s well suited to the way Puglia is at once Italy’s most rough and rustic region and also, in places, home to some truly spectacular examples of contemporary design. That’s the story here in Gagliano del Capo, at the very tip of the heel of Italy’s boot, where the Roman hotelier Gabriele Salini and the Puglian art collector Francesco Petrucci have transformed the 150-year-old Palazzo Daniele into a fantastically stylish (and incredibly small) luxury boutique hotel.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Six Senses Rome in Rome
ld.description: It’s not easy to build in a city as deeply historical as Rome, and many hoteliers are forced to make compromises. Once you’re at the level of a Six Senses, however, it seems anything is possible. Six Senses Rome, like so many other Roman hotels, occupies a historical palace, in this case the 15th-century Palazzo Salviati Cesi Mellini, a former cardinal’s residence whose exteriors and architecture have been meticulously restored and preserved.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Villa Cora in Florence
ld.description: Built by Baron Oppenheim for his bride in the nineteenth century, during Florence’s brief turn as Italy’s capital, Villa Cora still feels like a private residence. This neoclassical mansion sits on the outskirts of Florence, yet is still convenient to the city, near the Boboli Gardens and the Piazzale Michelangelo.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed (cleaning fee 80 EUR per stay).

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: J.K. Place Capri in Capri
ld.description: It’s exactly this sort of thing that drives home the point about how absurdly blessed Italy is as a travel destination. As if the original JK Place in Florence weren’t enough, they’ve gone and opened another one, in Capri. The choice now is between a smart urban boutique hotel in one of the world’s most beautiful cities, or an equally smart seaside boutique hotel, on one of the world’s most picturesque islands.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets up to 5kg are allowed on request. Charges apply.

award.awardFor: Three MICHELIN Keys · An extraordinary stay

ld.name: Monaci delle Terre Nere in Zafferana Etnea
ld.description: Plenty of Sicilian hotels boast of their views of Mount Etna, but few can quite match the situation of Monaci delle Terre Nere. That’s not just any terre nere, after all — this black earth is the volcanic stuff, and it’s no wonder, since here you’re literally on the slopes, albeit the safe lower slopes, of Sicily’s most salient geographic feature.
ld.petsAllowed: \n Small pets are allowed on an on-request basis (charges apply).

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Velona's Jungle Luxury Suites in Florence
ld.description: If we had a nickel for every pocket-sized jungle-themed luxury boutique hotel we’ve seen over the years, we’d have a grand total of five cents. Velona’s Jungle Luxury Suites is the only one of its kind, and much of that has to do with Velona himself. That’s Pasquale Velona, antique dealer and dear departed grandfather of the proprietor, Veronica Grechi — this hotel, just to the west of Florence’s busy city center, clearly contains generations’ worth of details.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed free of charge.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Precise Tale Poggio Alla Sala in Montepulciano
ld.description: Neither a straightforwardly typical Tuscan villa nor an iconoclastic experiment, Precise Tale Poggio Alla Sala is just unique enough: perfectly capable of delivering the classic experience that makes Tuscany a perennially desirable destination, but with a point of view that makes its version a particularly memorable one. It’s set amid cypress and olive groves on the rolling hills mere minutes from Montepulciano; inside, its designers took inspiration from the Silk Routes that once connected Italy to the far East, to create a style that’s local but heavily influenced by places as distant as Istanbul and Shanghai.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: J.K. Place Roma in Rome
ld.description: Florence and Capri aren’t exactly easy places to open a world-beating high-end boutique hotel. But by comparison, Rome is the big leagues. You can see why the minds behind JK Place wanted to wait until they could be assured of getting it right — and get it right they most certainly did.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed (free of charge).

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Castelfalfi in Montaione
ld.description: Charming as they are, rustic little farmhouses aren’t the only way to do Tuscany. Sometimes a full-on luxury resort is precisely what’s called for. In fact even that label fails to quite do justice to Castelfalfi, which is rather more like a luxury village, set on a 2,700-acre estate with commanding views of the surrounding valley, complete with vineyards, olive groves, multiple restaurants and bars.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Masseria Calderisi in Savelletri di Fasano
ld.description: Halfway from the town of Fasano to the beach, set on an estate that dates back to the 17th century, is Masseria Calderisi, a 24-room luxury boutique hotel that makes a strong case for the singular charms of southern Italian country hospitality.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Canne Bianche Lifestyle Hotel in Torre Canne di Fasano
ld.description: Puglia, as you may know, is enjoying its moment in the sun — it’s suddenly a hot destination among travelers seeking something a bit shinier and brighter than the traditional Tuscan escapade. (All puns in the preceding sentence are entirely intentional.) Canne Bianche Lifestyle Hotel, as the name implies, aims to be something more than just the latest addition to the boutique-hotel offerings dotting the so-called heel of the boot.
ld.petsAllowed: Small pets allowed on request at a charge to be paid locally.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Masseria Torre Coccaro in Savelletri di Fasano
ld.description: Puglia, in Italy’s southeast, is considered the new Tuscany. And the region has plenty to recommend it: gorgeous beaches, balmy weather, the intangible thrill of going against the grain, and some remarkable hotels — like the Masseria Torre Coccaro, less than an hour’s drive from both Bari and Brindisi.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Londra Palace Venezia in Venice
ld.description: It’s hard to beat this location; one entire side of the Hotel Londra Palace opens onto a stunning view of the lagoon and the island of San Giorgio, a view which, as the hotel is quick to point out, kept Tchaikovsky inspired during the creation of his Fourth Symphony.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Palazzo Margherita in Bernalda
ld.description: Francis Ford Coppola leaves his stamp on more than movies: wine, restaurants, literary magazines, and of course hotels carry the Coppola name as well. In the case of Palazzo Margherita, however, it’s more than a matter of defining his personal taste for a public audience. This 19th-century palazzo has deeply personal significance to the famed director, located as it is in the little-known southern Italian village of Bernalda, the birthplace of his grandfather, Agostino Coppola.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Hotel Locarno in Rome
ld.description: It’s easy to think of the boutique hotel as a fairly recent phenomenon, but Rome’s Hotel Locarno was serving up a uniquely eccentric brand of glamorous hospitality as early as the 1970s. As a guest house, it dates back even farther — the main building to 1925, when its Art Nouveau architectural style was the state of the art, and an adjacent villa all the way back to 1905. Thanks to constant attention by successive generations of proprietors, it’s kept itself splendidly up to date, and its multiple layers of history lend it a depth that other 21st-century boutique hotels would kill for.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets allowed on request (fee applies).

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: I Borghi dell'Eremo in Piegaro
ld.description: If you’ve got some facility with the Italian language you’ll have recognized that I Borghi dell’Eremo is plural. This is not a single farmhouse hotel, but three distinct “villages,” each one serving a different purpose for guests, but all constructed in a similar contemporary-classic style — and all with the same stunning views of the countryside on the border between Tuscany and Umbria.
ld.petsAllowed: \n Pets are allowed. Charges may be applicable.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Singer Palace Hotel Roma in Rome
ld.description: For Catholics, the heart of Rome may be Vatican City; for sightseers, the Spanish Steps or the Trevi Fountain. For shoppers, however, the heart of the Eternal City is the Via del Corso, with its boutiques and luxury-brand flagships. This was also the heart of Rome for the Singer sewing-machine company, which built the Singer Palace here at the height of its powers nearly a century ago. Those days are gone, but this Art Deco palazzo remains, transformed by a local architect and a Milanese interior designer into a small luxury hotel in the contemporary Roman style.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Vico Milano  in Milan
ld.description: Vico Milano is a small-scale hideaway by a family that also owns the Castello di Vicarello in Tuscany. More personal, yes, but no less stylish — its public spaces are dazzling, filled with design furniture and contemporary art, while its rooms and suites are handsome in a more relaxed way, delicately balanced between sparse simplicity and organic warmth.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

address.streetAddress: via la Stretta 231, Loc. Capezzano Pianore

ld.name: Locanda al Colle in Camaiore
ld.description: Not only are the Italians experts at living the good life, they’re also quite well versed in extracting maximum luxury from relatively humble means. Locanda al Colle is little more than a guesthouse in a village in coastal Tuscany, a short distance from Pisa and Lucca, whose nine rooms look out over forested hillsides through huge picture windows — but despite the lack of big-resort bells and whistles, you’d be hard pressed to catch guests wishing for much more than this.
ld.petsAllowed: \n Pets allowed at extra charge only in rooms with outdoor space.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Vocabolo Moscatelli in Umbertide
ld.description: It’s not just the name that marks Vocabolo Moscatelli Boutique Hotel & Restaurant as an “only in Italy” production — nowhere else on Earth do hoteliers so freely mix elements like the ancient stone walls of a 12th-century Umbrian monastery with ultra-modern, ultra-luxe designer furniture. The rooms are divided between the original structure and a newer annex, but all of them are artfully crafted, atmospheric, and more than a little bit luxurious. The hotel’s bar specializes in cocktails and local wines, while the restaurant serves high-end, creative Umbrian cuisine with global influences in a charming indoor-outdoor space.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Cascioni Eco Retreat in Costa Smeralda
ld.description: Not far from the Emerald Coast of northeastern Sardinia is a classic farmhouse complex that’s gone the way of so many Mediterranean farmhouses — transformed into a luxe and glamorous modern boutique hotel. Cascioni Eco Retreat is, as its name suggests, not just about luxury; its mission is to be a good steward of the land that it occupies, and to immerse its guests in the island’s considerable natural splendor.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Grand Hotel Victoria in Menaggio
ld.description: The Grand Hotel Victoria, like many of Lake Como’s luxury hotels, begins with neoclassical architecture, with a touch of the Liberty style that was current at its 19th-century founding, as well as an air of Old Hollywood glamour. But for all its historical influences, this is no museum piece: today’s Victoria is impressively renovated, and its interiors show evidence of a contemporary designer’s attentions, from the color work to the modern luxury furnishings and the subtle high-tech comforts.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Monastero Santa Rosa in Conca dei Marini
ld.description: A renovated 17th-century monastery is the stuff glamorously reclusive holidays are made of — especially in a destination as popular as the Amalfi Coast. The atmosphere of seclusion is supplied by the building and the site, while the Italian-style dolce vita is a result of the fact that the present-day Monastero Santa Rosa Hotel & Spa is focused not on renouncing pleasure, but embracing it.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Mediterraneo Sorrento in Sorrento
ld.description: Like its neighbors on the Amalfi Coast, Sorrento at its best is a destination that promises tranquil seclusion with a bit of drama — the cliffside setting of Sant’Agnello in particular makes for extraordinary views out to sea, as well as some memorably unusual topography. And the Hotel Mediterraneo Sorrento benefits from both — its terrace looks out across the Bay of Naples at the distant peak of Mt. Vesuvius.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Casa Clàt in Cagliari
ld.description: In the heart of Cagliari, mere minutes by foot from the marina quarter, is a luxury boutique hotel that shows an uncommonly refined side of the Sardinian capital. Artistic director Giorgio Casu has crafted a distinctive style that bridges different eras while incorporating the work of numerous Sardinian artists, designers, and craftspeople; Studio Pilia led the architectural design and renovation of the residence.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Stella d'Italia in Florence
ld.description: In a city full of impressive hotels, Stella d’Italia manages to stand out. It’s partly the location, inside an elegant 16th-century palazzo designed by Renaissance architect Giorgio Vasari; it’s just off the upscale Via de' Tornabuoni, a few minutes’ stroll from the Duomo. And it’s partly the contemporary intervention by a pair of creative Florentine hoteliers, designer Matteo Perduca and his calligrapher wife, Betty Soldi, already known for three other fashionable B&B-style properties around town. Their fourth collaboration is an ode to Italianità — the spirit of being Italian — with one-of-a-kind interiors featuring hundreds of original paintings, eclectic art objects, old film posters, and quirky antiques uncovered at local flea markets.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Nolinski Venezia - Evok Collection in Venice
ld.description: The Evok Collection is best known for its Parisian line of luxury boutique hotels, which include such gems as Brach, Sinner, and Cour des Vosges — as well as the original Nolinski. But the Evok approach is equally well suited to Venice, a city that’s just as heavily traveled, and which features its fair share of extravagant hotels. Nolinski Venezia, we’re happy to report, is further proof that there’s no necessary tradeoff between high luxury and high fashion — in the right hands, a hotel is perfectly capable of delivering both.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are welcome.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Palazzo Talìa in Rome
ld.description: The conversion of a 16th-century palazzo in the center of Rome into a luxury boutique hotel would be a noteworthy event on its own terms — the fact that Palazzo Talìa’s designer was none other than the film director Luca Guadagnino gives it a cultural resonance that few other hotels can match.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Villa Eden The Longevity Retreat in Merano
ld.description: The South Tyrol spa town of Merano has been a luxury travel destination for longer than the phrase “luxury travel destination” has existed; even against this backdrop, the aptly named Villa Eden stands out for its extraordinarily restorative atmosphere. Its setting, in an ornate Art Nouveau villa, feels like something out of a fairy tale, and its spa is no mere massage operation, but an intensively health-focused medical establishment specializing not just in relaxation but in longevity as well.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Monastero di Cortona in Cortona
ld.description: All of Cortona’s best hotels are located inside landmark buildings — palaces in town, country estates set amid vineyards — and the Monastero di Cortona Hotel & Spa is no exception. Indeed, this 15th-century monastery, with its gorgeous original frescoes, high vaulted ceilings, and breathtaking hilltop vantage point, may be the most impressive of them all. The imposing stone building was thoughtfully restored and transformed into a luxury boutique hotel in 2019, and it remains one of the most elegant lodgings in this corner of Tuscany.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: La Monastica Resort & Spa in Buggiano Castello
ld.description: The 16th-century Monastery of Santa Scolastica, once a treasure trove of beautiful frescoes and stained glass panels on a hilltop in Tuscany, has been altered and abandoned many times over the course of its history. Following years of painstaking restoration involving a team of historians, architects, and art conservators, the convent reopened as La Monastica Resort & Spa in 2024. The results are nothing short of spectacular: the original chapel has been transformed into an atmospheric restaurant, the old stone terraces now feature tiered gardens and swimming pools fringed by lemon trees, and the nuns’ humble quarters have been shaped into elegant rooms and suites with sweeping views over the valley below.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Monteverdi Tuscany in Castiglioncello del Trinoro
ld.description: Castiglioncello del Trinoro, a medieval village perched on a hilltop in Tuscany’s Val d’Orcia, was all but abandoned after the Second World War. Decades later, a vacationing American attorney fell in love with the place and started snapping up property, later tapping the Rome-based architect Ilaria Miani to turn a collection of old houses into a luxury boutique hotel. Today, Monteverdi Tuscany is part of the village, with ancient cobblestoned streets leading between guest rooms, a stone-walled swimming pool set, beautiful gardens, a spa and wellness center, a library, a terrace bar, an art gallery with rotating exhibitions from contemporary artists, a culinary academy, and a 14th-century church used as a concert venue.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Vista Verona in Verona
ld.description: Verona has been curiously underserved by the world’s high-end hoteliers, but the advent of Vista Verona rights that wrong; behind the relatively unassuming façade of a 19th-century building in the old city center are 16 extraordinary lavish rooms and suites, the work of the Milanese firm Maurizio Maggi Studio Arte. They’re the equal of just about any large-scale luxury hotel, and they come with services to match: a gorgeous private library, an indoor swimming pool, a spa and a well-equipped fitness center, and a spectacular rooftop terrace, which sits atop the penthouse-level restaurant and bar.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Palazzo Ripetta in Rome
ld.description: This 17th-century convent became a hotel in the 1960s, but it was only during its 2020 closure that Palazzo Ripetta found its present form — a family-owned luxury hotel with a strong visual identity (and an enviable collection of art). The location, two streets to the south of the Piazza del Popolo, could hardly be more auspicious, and the 78 rooms and suites are the very picture of modern Roman elegance. Piazzetta Ripetta is open all day for drinks and light snacks while restaurant San Baylon serves classic Roman dishes. Up on the rooftop locals and visitors alike gather over unique cocktails with a view of the city.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Adler Ritten in Soprabolzano
ld.description: Adler Ritten occupies a wooded Alpine glade just outside Bolzano, Italy, where Italian and German cultures intermingle freely in the shadow of the Dolomites. The concept is a timeless one, as is the execution; the style blends the region’s typical warmth with confident contemporary design. It’s a winning formula, with storybook vistas that can be seen from all over the property, including the all-season infinity pool and the extensive wellness complex.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Relais Roncolo 1888 in Quattro Castella
ld.description: Emilia-Romagna’s first wine and balsamic relais, Roncolo 1888 is set within the organic Tenuta Venturini Baldini estate outside Quattro Castella, with vineyards, balsamic acetaia, and kitchen gardens all on the property. The historic Villa Manodori dates to 1670, and rooms across the villa and surrounding borgo buildings mix wood-beamed ceilings with mid-century furniture, iron four-poster beds, and pops of color. The greenhouse restaurant cooks from the estate’s own harvest. You're also squarely in Italy's Motor Valley, Ferrari country, for those who want to take a detour from the dinner table.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Leonardo Trulli Resort in Locorotondo
ld.description: The conical structures known as trulli are among the most distinctive of Puglia’s traditional building forms, and it’s perhaps unsurprising that Leonardo Trulli Resort leans all the way in to the charm of these whitewashed stone buildings. It’s set on the outskirts of Locorotondo, an inland town midway between Bari and Brindisi, and it benefits from the pastoral tranquility of its rural setting.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: LA ROQQA in Porto Ercole
ld.description: LA ROQQA brings a sharp new energy to Porto Ercole, a once-sleepy port town on Tuscany’s Argentario coast. Perched above the harbor with views across the bay, it’s a contemporary retreat wrapped in saturated color, sculptural design, and just the right amount of seaside glamour. Rooms are calm and sun-filled, with tactile details: think Ortigia products, terrazzo accents, and Italian-made everything. The rooftop is the hotel’s social anchor, home to Scirocco, a standout restaurant where seafood and sunset cocktails come with a front-row seat to the harbor, and just a ten-minute walk away is the hotel's seasonal beach club Isolotto where guests can dine, drink, and laze away summer days.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Villa Petriolo in Cerreto Guidi
ld.description: Villa Petriolo is a restored estate in the Tuscan countryside, where Renaissance architecture meets a deep commitment to the land. Once a noble residence, it now functions as both a warm retreat and working farm, with suites housed across former agricultural buildings and hillside villas. Three restaurants offer everything from traditional Tuscan fare to more inventive dishes, all rooted in the estate’s own harvest. Guests can join wine tastings, meditate in the gardens, or explore the grounds at their own pace. It is an escape that feels grounded, generous, and completely transformative.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: L’Andana in Castiglione della Pescaia
ld.description: L’Andana occupies a particularly auspicious parcel of land near western Tuscany’s Tyrrhenian coast — Tenuta La Badiola was once the summer residence of the Grand Duke Leopold II, and today is as picturesque a collection of vineyards and sun-drenched foothills as one is likely to find anywhere in Italy. Here you’re remote enough to hide out for a while, if that’s your style, yet equally well placed to see the sights, near enough to places like Siena and Lucca and the scenic Maremma coast to make for easy day-tripping.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Borgo Egnazia in Savelletri di Fasano
ld.description: There’s not a lot of green on the sun-drenched Puglian coast, but the San Domenico golf course is a notable exception. And just off the course, surrounded by gardens and olive groves, is the sort of full-spectrum hotel that’s equally uncommon in this part of the country — the Borgo Egnazia.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Borgo San Felice Resort in Castelnuovo Berardenga
ld.description: On a hilltop in Chianti, with views of Siena on the horizon and vines and oaks in the middle distance, just about an entire village has been converted into a luxury hotel, the only exceptions being the residences of the farmers who tend the vineyards. May as well read that sentence just once more before you make your reservation. This is the Borgo San Felice; this, more generally, is why people never get tired of going to Tuscany.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed (only small-size dogs, not in common areas, upon request and availability). Supplement 50 EUR.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Anantara Palazzo Naiadi Rome in Rome
ld.description: Many of Rome’s finest hotels are on the smaller side, but not this one: the Anantara Palazzo Naiadi Rome Hotel is a proper full-scale grand hotel, a 232-room monument behind a neoclassical façade facing the Piazza della Repubblica.
ld.petsAllowed: Please note dogs and cats are allowed, max. weight 25kg. Limited availability, please contact the hotel before booking. A charge of 50€ per day will be applied (max. 2 pets per room). Guide dogs free of charge.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Capri Tiberio Palace  in Capri
ld.description: Italy is strewn with jaw-dropping destinations — it’s hardly fair that the Amalfi Coast and the Gulf of Naples should find themselves joined by no less scenic a neighbor than Capri. It seems a bit greedy to be hoarding all that seaside majesty, which probably explains why the Roman Emperor Tiberius established his villa on the island. Today, of course, Capri caters to visitors with a slightly less reclusive bent. With its status as one of the world’s most beguiling hotspots firmly established, the island plays host to a number of remarkably low-key yet jazzy hotels, of which the Capri Tiberio Palace is a stunning example.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Borgo Santo Pietro in Chiusdino
ld.description: In a manner of speaking, Borgo Santo Pietro could be considered a design hotel. It’s just that the design in question is thoroughly thirteenth-century. Sometimes, it turns out, the old ways are the best ways, and it just so happens that this statement is more often true in Tuscany than perhaps anywhere else. So in spite of the youth of its Danish owners, not to mention the state-of-the-art modern luxuries on offer, the Borgo Santo Pietro, in the countryside outside of Siena, has opted for an atmosphere that’s utterly antique — if you silence your mobile phone and hide the eminently hideable flat-screen television, you could just about convince yourself you’re living in the Renaissance.

award.awardFor: Three MICHELIN Keys · An extraordinary stay

ld.name: Castello Banfi - Il Borgo in Montalcino
ld.description: At Castello Banfi Wine Resort, the 14-room boutique hotel is only the keep to this Tuscan castle-on-a-hill — the castello is the headquarters of the working wine estate, while the borgo is the boutique hotel that’s been fashioned from the adjoining village buildings. If the property ended at the sandstone walls, it would still be a must-visit for anyone passing through the countryside near Siena. Thankfully, there’s also the small matter of a nearly two-thousand-acre vineyard, sloping gently down from the fortress to meet the surrounding valley — and it’s worth knowing that your stay includes a tasting, a vineyard and winery tour with the sommelier, and a discount at the hotel’s wine shop.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Relais Blu in Massa Lubrense
ld.description: The icy color palettes and minimalist furniture that were once urban-boutique staples take on a whole new meaning outside the bright-lights, big-city context. Transplant that crisp look to an olive and pine grove at the tip of the Sorrentine Peninsula, for example, and you’ve got a fresh take on Mediterranean style. This kind of modernism really benefits from the warming contrast of a healthy dose of old-world seaside glamour, and the 11-room Relais Blu is running a master class in this particular fusion.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Palazzo Avino in Ravello
ld.description: A thousand feet high on a hilltop in Ravello, with a spectacular view of the Amalfi Coast, Palazzo Avino is at once charmingly ancient and sparklingly new: while this 12th-century palace has been one of Europe’s top hotels, in various forms, since the 1880s, its most recent renovation leaves it looking beautifully ageless, its rooms and suites a heady blend of antique styles and focused contemporary colors. Eclectic artworks, many of them modern and contemporary, add another dimension of visual depth; none of it, however, distracts from the astonishing views.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: The First Arte, Rome in Rome
ld.description: Here, just off the Via del Corso, at the First Roma Arte - by the Pavilions Hotels, you’re most comfortably ensconced in the sort of small luxury hotel, where near-impossible refinement and cozy residential atmosphere go naturally hand in hand. And then, on top of that, the place is simply drenched in art.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets allowed for extra 100 EUR per stay.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Grand Hotel Parker's in Naples
ld.description: Naples is probably best known for its thrillingly chaotic urbanity, but the Grand Hotel Parker's belongs to another side of the city — the side exemplified by the graceful curve of the waterfront, the splendid architectural treasures, and the hilly neighborhood slopes, like stadium seating for the blue Mediterranean stage set to the south.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Hotel Signum in Salina
ld.description: Scientists look at Sicily and see volcanic landforms, geothermal sites and ongoing geologic land-creation, the building of the earth itself. For anyone seeking to indulge their inner volcanologist, there’s not much left to say. But for the rest of us there’s the Hotel Signum. A marriage between boutique hotel and Aeolian farmhouse, the Signum holds its own as a well-designed, memorable experience on the precipice of one of the most unique landscapes in the world.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Grand Hotel et de Milan in Milan
ld.description: Milan may be the most fashion-forward city in Italy, the couture capital, and the center of industrial progress as well—but this is still Italy, after all, and there’s always room for a little bit of ancient history. Nothing industrial or futuristic about it: the Grand Hotel et de Milan is every bit as traditionally elegant as the La Scala theater, which is just a few steps away—and this location surely played a crucial role in the hotel’s history, as such famous names as Nureyev, Callas, and Caruso have graced its guestbook.
ld.petsAllowed: \n Pets are allowed on request free of charge.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: The Ashbee Hotel in Taormina
ld.description: Built steps away from the ruins of an ancient Greek theater, perched on a cliff overlooking the Ionian Sea, with a garden full of citrus trees, the Ashbee would almost be too insistently Sicilian, too steadfastly true to its type, if it weren’t for its English heritage. Instead it’s lent a charming dose of eccentricity by its history as the villa of a British colonel who retired here in the first decade of the 20th century.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Principe Forte dei Marmi in Forte dei Marmi
ld.description: The glassy, angular, decidedly modern Principe Fortei dei Marmi is Tuscan Riviera to the utmost, as unapologetically glamorous as a hotel can be without slipping over into ostentation. It’s not so much a beach hotel as a riviera hotel, more butler-served day-bed cabanas than flip-flops and sandy toes. It’s also a very pleasant reminder that all those sea breezes wafting toward the vineyards and villas to the east had to come from somewhere, and that somewhere turns out to be a stunning rocky coast with a scene all its own — stylish seaside restaurants and late-night dance parties sharing the land’s end with laid-back beach strollers and Florentines escaping from the city.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Villa Crespi in Orta San Giulio
ld.description: You could be forgiven for thinking there’s nothing really all that out of the ordinary about Villa Crespi, but only if you had a good reason for thinking it was in Istanbul. As it stands, Villa Crespi is in the north of Italy, less than an hour from Milan, on the shores of Lake Orta — which makes this hyper-opulent Moorish-style palace (minaret and all) one of Italy’s strangest and most extraordinary small hotels.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed at Villa Crespi.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: La Barchessa di Villa Pisani in Bagnolo di Lonigo
ld.description: There are Palladian villas, and then there are Palladian villas. Villa Pisani isn’t just Palladian in style, it was designed by the 16th-century architect Andrea Palladio himself, and for fans of Renaissance architecture, there’s no higher endorsement for a stay at La Barchessa di Villa Pisani. (Not to mention its Shakespearean location in the Veneto, between Verona and Padua.)

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Bellevue Hotel & Spa in Cogne
ld.description: As Alpine resorts go, Cogne is low-key. Though close to the Swiss border and within easy reach of the Piedmont wine region, it’s tucked away in a quiet and relatively undeveloped corner of the Aosta Valley, on the edge of Italy’s oldest national park, the fittingly named Gran Paradiso. It’s not, in other words, the kind of place where new boutique hotels are opening every season. Bellevue Hotel & Spa, for instance, is a family-owned, and it’s been in business for almost a century — just after the park was founded, even before the concept of a modern ski resort existed around here.
ld.petsAllowed: Dogs are welcome in some particular rooms with stone floor. Other pets are not allowed.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Paragon 700 Boutique Hotel & SPA in Ostuni
ld.description: If your iconic image of a holiday in Puglia is the minimalism of a white masseria nestled in an olive grove, then Paragon 700 might not be for you. But if you like to be surprised and a bit unsettled, with its bold modernity, this irreverent, provocative, and decidedly unconventional hotel will show you a different aspect of this region.
ld.petsAllowed: - Pets are allowed with an additional charge

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Gardena Grödnerhof Hotel & Spa in Ortisei
ld.description: The Dolomites are home to lodges of all descriptions, from quaint old wooden contraptions to ultra-modern eco-lodges. But there’s nothing else quite like the Gardena Grödnerhof Gourmet & Spa Hotel. Constructed in 1923, it’s about as ornate as these things can be; a 21st-century restoration left its majestic silhouette intact, even as it updated its color palette and its interior finishes.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are not allowed.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

pages.h1: Splendido Mare, A Belmond Hotel, Portofino

ld.name: Splendido Mare, A Belmond Hotel, Portofino in Portofino
ld.description: Portofino has some fabulous hotels, but only a few of them are set on the town’s charming central piazza, one of the most photographed spots on the impossibly picturesque Italian Riviera. Splendido Mare is one of them, and it’s a toss-up whether it’s more pleasant inside or out. The boutique hotel is tucked into a row of pastel-colored buildings on the cobblestoned Piazza Martiri dell’Olivetta, with its fragrant citrus trees, open-air cafés, and white sailboats bobbing in the harbor just steps away. Stepping through the front door, you’ll find Splendido Mare colorful and chic: redesigned by Studio Festen in 2021, the décor takes inspiration from the village’s nautical history and the retro glamour of its midcentury heyday.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Ansitz Steinbock in Villandro
ld.description: Ansitz Steinbock comes by its stone walls honestly. This sturdy structure’s foundations were laid in the 13th century, and while it’s been thoroughly renovated by hotelier Elisabeth Rabensteiner, its historical aspect is the first thing you’ll notice. The setting is the mountain village of Villandro, or Villanders, not far from Bolzano; the cuisine in the eponymous fine dining restaurant is pure South Tyrol, accompanied by Alto Adige wines.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Grand Hotel Tremezzo in Tremezzina
ld.description: "That sunny, happy place"—that's how Greta Garbo described the Grand Hotel Tremezzo in the 1932 film Grand Hotel. And who could possibly disagree?
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed. No extra charges.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Villa d'Este in Cernobbio
ld.description: Villa D’Este is one of the world’s most famous grand hotels, and deservedly so. This villa built in 1568 has been a hotel for almost as long as the modern, unified Republic of Italy has existed — the first guest checked in in 1873 — and the transition from aristocratic residence to opulent grand hotel was a natural one.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Conti di San Bonifacio in Gavorrano
ld.description: Conti di San Bonifacio is a beautifully renovated seven-room farmhouse on a hill, surrounded by several hundred acres of vineyards, olive groves and rolling woods. Anywhere but Tuscany, that might be enough, the hotelier’s work done and the guests lining up to take their heavy doses of endorphins. Here amidst one of the world’s great concentrations of impossibly pleasurable hotels, however, it takes something more — like bathrooms carved from marble and bedrooms draped in furs, say.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Portrait Roma in Rome
ld.description: The flagship Ferragamo store would already be something of a holy place, if you’re into that sort of thing. Less well known, but possibly more exciting, is what’s upstairs, in the top floors of this 19th-century townhouse: the Portrait Roma, the boutique hotels by Lungarno, the Ferragamo family’s hospitality concern.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed. Charges apply.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Ottolire Resort in Locorotondo
ld.description: Puglia offers an alternative vision of Italian country living: rugged, sun-bleached hills, dotted with olive groves, and rough-hewn stone buildings that manage to feel elegant and rustic in roughly equal measure. Come to think of it, that’s an apt enough description of Ottolire Resort, a 13-room luxury boutique hotel in the Valle d’Itria, just under an hour from Bari.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

pages.h1: Lefay Resort & Spa Lago di Garda

ld.name: Lefay Resort & Spa Lago di Garda in Gargnano
ld.description: Lefay Resort specializes in environmentally sensitive, extraordinarily well-appointed balm for souls made weary by the world. How well appointed? It’s got multiples not just of swimming pools, but also saunas, meditation gardens, and relaxation areas, on top of 25 acres of parkland for anything from running to lounging. If you’re looking to detox or revamp, you can’t do much better than this secluded mountaintop retreat — and the views of Lake Garda certainly don’t hurt either.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Critabianca in Cutrofiano
ld.description: It’s an unusually cosmopolitan story: set in Grecìa Salentina, an enclave of Greek descent in the tip of the heel of Puglia, Critabianca was established as a farmhouse in the 14th century, and then transformed into an aristocratic residence by a French nobleman during a period of 18th-century Bourbon rule. Today it’s a classic country-house hotel, and a perfect introduction to the charms of southern Italian life, convenient to the beaches and to towns like Gallipoli, Otranto, and Lecce.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Masseria della Volpe in Noto
ld.description: The Province of Syracuse doesn’t need much to improve on its native panoramic grandeur: a few plates of fresh eats, room to walk around, something hearty to decant, and the silence in which to contemplate it all. A restored 19th-century manor farm sums those right up, if we do say so ourselves, and Masseria della Volpe fits the bill nicely. Set on a verdant, rambly patch of earth southwest of Noto, it’s a fine example of la dolce vita Siciliana; with vineyard-bearing, weathered limestone hills in one direction and the untroubled Ionian Sea glinting in the other, it’s close to the dictionary definition.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Seven Rooms Villadorata in Noto
ld.description: In 1774, Corrado Nicolaci was granted the title of Prince of Villadorata, and his palace in Noto became a showcase of the family’s prestige. Set in the historic heart of Noto, it’s the kind of place that could easily feel overly formal or grandiose. But the owner has gone to great lengths to make this palatial Baroque-style residence feel warm and personable in addition to being, well, drop-dead gorgeous. Frescoed ceilings, stately columns, furnishings by the best Italian designers, check, check and check. But thanks to smart planning and attention to detail, there are also countless quaint and cozy spaces waiting to be discovered.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are not allowed.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Lefay Resort & Spa Dolomiti in Pinzolo
ld.description: Le Corbusier once described the craggy peaks of the Dolomites as “the most beautiful work of architecture ever seen.” Lefay Resort & SPA Dolomiti, the first major luxury resort in the Madonna di Campiglio skiarea, pays tribute to these surroundings. Built in 2019, this modernist mountain hideaway features sharp lines, wooden accents, and soaring floor-to-ceiling pyramid windows that let the outside in. Rooms, which include wall-mounted fireplaces and private terraces or balconies, are the perfect place to admire views of the valley below. While guests will certainly explore the vast expanse of Madonna di Campiglio’s ski trails and snowboard parks, they might also be tempted to pause for a moment and enjoy the hotel’s massive spa, whose four floors and outdoor area include a saltwater lake, nine saunas, and a whirlpool containing magnesium salts for muscle relaxation.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Siena House in Torrita di Siena
ld.description: For all their other charms, Italian hotels, as a rule, don’t really do understatement — so when you find a place that’s confident enough simply to call itself Siena House, it’s a good bet there’s something a bit special going on. (The proprietors are British, in fact, which goes a long way, now that we think of it, towards explaining the understatement.)

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Lùme in Syracuse
ld.description: Ortigia, the historic heart of the city of Siracusa, is the setting for Lùme, a six-bedroom boutique bed and breakfast owned by a Parisian hotelier that nevertheless showcases this Italian city in as flattering a light as anything by a local. At this size, it’s a relatively simple matter to furnish a hotel with the warmth and intimacy of a private home; what’s more remarkable is to combine that feeling with the sophisticated stylishness that’s on display at Lùme.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Donna Coraly Country Boutique Hotel in Syracuse
ld.description: Not far from Syracuse, along the southeastern coast of Sicily, the 14th-century San Michele family estate is home to the small and luxurious Donna Coraly Country Boutique Hotel. A few low-profile buildings — once used to house farm workers — have been thoughtfully transformed into guest accommodations. While not original to the estate, the hotel was designed in a style that harmonizes with its surroundings, blending centuries-old architectural influences with modern and contemporary art and design.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Villa La Massa in Florence
ld.description: When it comes to hotels, Italy — and Tuscany in particular — is among the world’s most fertile destinations. To say, then, that the Villa La Massa is among the region’s hidden gems is high praise indeed. With just 51 rooms and suites it’s edging into real boutique territory, and its location is among Italy’s most desirable — it stands just outside of Florence, overlooking the Arno river and the Chianti Valley, surrounded by twenty-two acres of parkland just a few minutes outside of town and yet splendidly secluded amid the rolling Tuscan hills.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Corte di Gabriela in Venice
ld.description: In Venice, tourists might outnumber residents, but staying in the bustling heart of the city isn’t likely to diminish your experience — especially when the bustling heart in question happens to be San Marco, home of the Rialto Bridge and St. Mark’s Square. Don’t be a contrarian about it: this place is popular for some very good reasons. And what makes the eleven-room Corte di Gabriela so inviting, besides its location, is that it finds inventive ways to work within the Euro-boutique framework — yes, it’s a refurbished 19th-century building, but it plays with Venetian tropes to create an atmosphere of design-hotel chic, offering a luxurious experience that never takes itself too seriously.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Borgo dei Conti Resort in Boschetto Vecchio
ld.description: Borgo dei Conti Resort is a deeply romantic place, in that particular way that only a grand Southern European country house can be. Originally built as a fortress in the 13th century, the estate was remade into a noble home some 500 years later. Surrounded by acres of gardens and lawns and parkland, the building is a dramatic example of 19th-century neo-Gothic architecture, still as imposing as ever today.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Lido Palace in Riva del Garda
ld.description: Lido Palace just squeaks into the 19th-century club, founded in 1899 — but it’s got more than enough historic cred to justify its status, having hosted such Belle Époque names as Archduke Franz Ferdinand, King Vittorio Emanuele, and Cornelius Vanderbilt. The hotel’s palatial aspect never went away — it’s just been radically transformed by Alberto Cecchetto’s avant-architectural genius. The lobby, for instance, juts out from the edifice proper, a museum-like extension with a partitioned glass ceiling and swank neon seating. Or take the dining enclosure, a glass-and-metal marvel stretching nearly to the lake.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Palazzo Pascal in Scala
ld.description: Italy’s Amalfi Coast suffers from no shortage of spectacular views; even beyond Positano, places like Amalfi or Ravello or (a little higher up the hill) the tiny hamlet of Minuta look out over the same Tyrrhenian Sea from similarly lofty mountainside perches. It’s here that the Palazzo Pascal has stood since the 11th century, first as an aristocratic residence and now as a luxurious but low-key and thoroughly tranquil seven-suite boutique hotel, owned and operated by a creative family with exquisite taste in curation and collection.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: VIVERE Suites and Rooms in Arco
ld.description: Here, as in so many places across Italy, hoteliers struggle against the expectations created by their country’s treasured history. Ask anyone for their mental picture of a stay on the Lago di Garda and chances are the word “villa” will feature prominently. The flip side, of course, is that there’s a tidy living to be made subverting expectations — and a quick look at Vivere Suites and Rooms confirms that this is not exactly the postcard version of the Italian lake country.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Lagació Hotel Mountain Residence in San Cassiano
ld.description: We’re open about our admiration for Europe’s modernist ski lodges — but even so, Lagació Mountain Residence stands out. Too often, when updating the classic Alpine-lodge look, the temptation is to push things too far. When ski hotels start resembling high-altitude nightclubs, it’s easy to forget that warmth — in every sense — is the very essence of a mountain retreat.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Lake Spa Hotel SEELEITEN in Kaltern
ld.description: There’s nothing that catches the eye of a mountain-hotel aficionado quite like an Italian hotel with a German name. It’s the sort of thing that only happens in South Tyrol, the Alpine corner of Italy. About midway between Verona and Innsbruck, Austria, not far from Bolzano, is where you’ll find the Lake Spa Hotel Seeleiten. It’s set by the side of Lake Caldaro, in a spectacular wine-producing valley surrounded on all sides by mountain peaks.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed on request. Charges may be applicable.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: La Fiermontina Luxury Home in Lecce
ld.description: In Lecce, the Baroque jewel of the Salentine peninsula, this luxurious little hotel is a tribute to the memory of Antonia Fiermonte, the owners’ grandmother, an artist and extraordinary woman who lived in the first half of the 20th century. The estate on which La Fiermontina Luxury Home stands can trace its roots to the 16th century, and the house itself to the 17th. It’s been substantially rebuilt, however, with the help of the local architect Antonio Annicchiarico; what stands here today is a tribute to the arches and vaults of the classic Pugliese masseria, but a thoroughly modern one.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed on request. Charges may be applicable.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Portrait Milano in Milan
ld.description: The long-awaited Portrait Milano joins its Lungarno Collection sisters in Rome and Florence, and it’s no surprise that for the brand’s first foray into the Italian fashion capital, it’s dressed for the occasion. The location could hardly be more suited to the purpose; this villa is hidden away within a large block right in the heart of the luxury-brand nexus that is the Golden Quadrangle, overlooking the colonnaded Piazza del Quadrilatero. And the hotel itself, as you can see, is a stunner — this 16th-century seminary has been masterfully transformed by the Ferragamo family’s designer of choice, Michele Bönan.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed for a fee of 50 EUR per stay.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Hotel Miramalfi in Amalfi
ld.description: It’s an age-old question whether it’s preferable to stay on the beach or on the hill overlooking it.
