A small spa by the banks of the Lesse provides further avenues for relaxation, and the landscape is ripe for exploration.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Corinthia Grand Hotel Astoria Brussels in Brussels
ld.description: Corinthia Grand Hotel Astoria Brussels was built in 1909 in a Beaux-Arts style, just in time for the Brussels Exposition of 1910. It laid empty for many years before being restored, reborn, and relaunched by the Corinthia Hotel Group in 2024. The sympathetic and detailed renovation work is best exemplified by the stunning Palm Court with its stained-glass skylight, while the 126 bedrooms blend classical elegance with modern facilities and contemporary levels of comfort.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: 1898 The Post & Porter’s House in Ghent
ld.description: Though completed at the turn of the last century, thanks to its neo-Gothic style Ghent’s old Central Post Office looks hundreds of years older than that. You don’t come to this part of Belgium in search of hyper-modern architectural experiments — you come in search of history, and 1898 The Post, a contemporary renovation of this beautifully preserved structure, has got a bit more than its fair share.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Hotel De Witte Lelie in Antwerp
ld.description: There are hotels that bowl you over with their undeniable hotel-ness: the doorman, the bellhop, the smiling concierge and the hustling waiters, pushing room service carts up and down the corridors. And then there are places that are barely hotels at all, little more than a comfortable and exquisitely designed guest house, trading all the pomp for a more personal charm, privacy and intimacy.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: The Notary in Bruges
ld.description: It’s not often thought of as one of the most glamorous professions, but the 19th-century notary who lived at Moerstraat 54 in Bruges had impeccable taste; the old family residence is now a lovely little nine-suite luxury bed and breakfast. The Notary is not just well-preserved but has been in many places improved; the antique atmosphere remains intact, but turning its existing rooms into modern guest suites was no small task.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Hotel Flora in Antwerp
ld.description: Occupying a few historic townhouses that were once the homes of 15th-century merchants, Hotel Flora is a gem of a hotel in medieval Antwerp. Pun not necessarily intended — despite the fact that the seven suites are named after precious stones. True to its concept, the hotel is vibrant, elegant, and one-of-a-kind, a walk-in treasure chest with a cozy vintage library, lush topiary, clawfoot tubs, and a colorful mural hand-painted by the Belgian landscape artist Nils Verkaeren. Original details like marble fireplaces and a decorative gatehouse only add to the appeal. It’s a sophisticated spot, and no kids are allowed, so the breakfast room is silent, cocktails in the lounge are uninterrupted, and the quiet courtyard garden stays that way.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Cobergher Hotel in Kortrijk
ld.description: Cobergher Hotel Kortrijk’s eclectic interior design stands in stark contrast to its 16th-century exterior; what’s now a modern boutique hotel was designed by the Dutch architect Wenceslas Coberghe in a conservative Gothic style. Its rooms range from classical — think period-style furnishings and chandeliers — to contemporary, such as the minimally dressed “Glorious” rooms with their clean lines and their timeless black-and-white palette. A collection of flats serves long-stay guests, and everyone benefits from a small spa area with a hammam, sauna and massage room, an afternoon tea service five days a week, and Bar Mémoir for cocktail hour.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

pages.h1: Pillows Grand Boutique Hotel Reylof Ghent

ld.name: Pillows Grand Boutique Hotel Reylof Ghent in Ghent
ld.description: Ghent did well to pedestrianize its historic city center: in so scenic a city, walking (or biking) allows time to linger with longing over its sumptuous frontage. Right in the thick of it all sits Pillows Grand Boutique Hotel Reylof Ghent, spanning a 1724 townhouse and its 20th-century neighbor — a union which is almost a perfect metaphor for the contemporary boutique hotel, balancing local authenticity and personal intimacy with global, forward-looking standards of service.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: La Réserve Knokke-Heist in Knokke-Heist
ld.description: Steps from the North Sea in the resort town of Knokke-Heist, Hotel La Réserve hosted a high society crowd in its mid-century heyday — past guests include Frank Sinatra, René Magritte, and Brigitte Bardot. The landmark reopened in 2023 following a design overhaul by the celebrated Belgian architect Glenn Sestig.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Kasteel van Ordingen in Sint-Truiden
ld.description: Amid the rolling hills and orchards of Limburg, Kasteel van Ordingen is a privately restored castle with deep medieval roots. Once held by the Teutonic Order, the estate was brought back to life over 21 years by owner Richard Sleurs, with interiors by Pieter Porters that highlight period details without feeling overly formal. Restaurant Aurum brings contemporary cooking to this marvelous setting, and Bistro Richard serves regional classics in the attractive and historic courtyard. Guests can head out by e-bike or Vespa to explore the roads and farmland that surround the estate.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are not allowed.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Hôtel Amigo in Brussels
ld.description: Once a jail, later a rather uninspired hotel, today’s refurbished Hotel Amigo (courtesy of Rocco Forte) is one of the best hotels in Brussels, for business or pleasure. The location is central, steps from the scenic Grand Place, in a pedestrian-only historic district, near enough to any number of shops, restaurants, the financial district, and even the Town Hall. And the hotel itself is sublime—a Spanish Renaissance building decorated with ancient Brussels flagstones, Magritte and Broodthaers prints, and even illustrations by Tintin creator Hergé.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Hotel Van Cleef in Bruges
ld.description: Ring the bell and enter the lobby, ready to admire the inimitable charm of the Van Cleef. A characterful hotel whose dimensions are such that it can offer a tailor - made experience to each guest. Enjoy your à la carte breakfast on the terrace by the canal. Superb!

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Boutiquehotel 't Fraeyhuis in Bruges
ld.description: Bordering Bruges’ fairytale Minnewater Park, Boutiquehotel ’t Fraeyhuis is a thorough reinvention of a centuries-old manor. Formerly Hotel Egmond, it still carries traces of its Renaissance past - with a grand fireplace here, and exposed beams there - now paired with stone floors, moody photography, and modern design. The garden bar, situated behind a glass-walled lounge, draws locals as much as guests. With just 12 individually styled rooms, this former noble residence feels private, cultured, and perfectly at home in the city of romance.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Dukes' Palace Brugge in Bruges
ld.description: Built by the Duke of Burgundy to mark his royal marriage, this 15th-century palace is now Bruges’ most opulent stay, and its only five-star hotel set within a former chateau. At Dukes’ Palace Brugge, history hasn’t been dusted away but carefully layered with comfort: original oil paintings, chandeliers, and stained glass sit easily alongside marble bathrooms and heated floors. Tapestry-toned rooms overlook sculpted gardens dotted with contemporary art, while the bistro and spa offer indulgences fit for nobility, past or present.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Juliana Hotel Brussels in Brussels
ld.description: Though it occupies a rather monumental Neoclassical building facing the Place des Martyrs, Juliana Hotel Brussels is residential in its scale and its atmosphere. This is a luxury boutique hotel, with equal emphasis on boutique and luxury — its spaces are generous and its comforts are high-end, and the design is nothing if not memorable. There’s art everywhere, both in the public spaces and in the rooms, where classic architectural gestures like mansard roofs and timbered ceilings are complemented by murals and modern design flourishes. The spa, with its indoor pool, is another inspired space, as are the swanky restaurant and the dramatically low-lit bar.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: De Durgerdam in Amsterdam
ld.description: It’s just 15 minutes by car (or 20 by bike) from Amsterdam proper, but those few minutes make all the difference in the world. De Durgerdam is convenient enough to the museums and other in-town destinations but trades the bustle of Amsterdam’s dense city center for a lakeside idyll, and elbow-to-elbow canal houses for a row of freestanding clapboard houses. The one containing De Durgerdam was, from the 17th century on, a fisherman’s inn — now, with some help from a modern addition, it’s a 14-room luxury boutique hotel with personality and atmosphere to spare.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: De L'Europe Amsterdam in Amsterdam
ld.description: One of just a few hotels that uphold the tradition of the classic European grand hotel, De L’Europe Amsterdam has been in business since 1896. And while it’s kept itself continually updated throughout the decades — most recently undergoing a thorough renovation in 2020 — the intent was never to reinvent the place, but to maintain the sense of timeless luxury that’s long been its signature. In fact a guest from a century ago might feel right at home here, once certain high-tech amenities had been adequately explained.

award.awardFor: Three MICHELIN Keys · An extraordinary stay

ld.name: Château St. Gerlach in Valkenburg
ld.description: At the edge of the Ingendael Nature Preserve, beyond the city center of Maastricht, sits a 15th-century monastery transformed into a Dutch countryside luxury hotel. Portions of Château St. Gerlach’s original farmhouse, convent, and grain lofts are now occupied by 114 guestrooms decorated in a country-chic style, plus residences for larger parties. There’s a Roman-style indoor pool, as well as a small spa with a sauna and turkish bath. Burgemeester Quicx is the hotel’s modern coffeehouse, while contemporary French classics are served in the exquisite dining room at Les Salons.
ld.petsAllowed: \n Pets are allowed. Charges may be applicable.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Central Park Voorburg  in The Hague
ld.description: The stately white building that houses Central Park Voorburg, one of the finest historic hotels in the Randstad, is called Vreugd & Rust — Dutch for “Peace & Rest.” The surrounding green space shares the same name, and it’s easy to see why. This country estate, just a stone’s throw from the Hague, is a national monument that doubles as a boutique hotel, with an elegant bar and restaurant suited to special occasions.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

pages.h1: Pillows Grand Boutique Hotel Maurits at the Park

ld.name: Pillows Grand Boutique Hotel Maurits at the Park in Amsterdam
ld.description: Even in summer, there’s a crisp, collegiate, fall-is-in-the-air atmosphere at the Pillows Grand Boutique Hotel Maurits at the Park. It’s an impression that makes perfect sense when you learn that this luxury boutique hotel makes its home inside a restored university building that dates back to 1908. With its elegant brick facade, high-arching ceilings, and large windows overlooking Amsterdam’s leafy Oosterpark, it’s more like the movie version of academia, and its light-filled rooms, with bespoke beds, heated floors, and Diptyque bath products, are a far cry from a college dorm. The best suite even has a grand piano and a marble bathroom with a soaking tub. Complimentary snacks and drinks are available around the clock in the modern guest lounge, and a collection of restaurants and bars — including a chic brasserie and a roaring twenties-style cocktail lounge named after F. Scott Fitzgerald — add to the appeal.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed. Charges may apply.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Château Neercanne in Maastricht
ld.description: High above the Jeker Valley, Château Neercanne stands out as the Netherlands’ only terraced castle, with formal Baroque gardens and a past that dates back to the 17th century. Built in 1698 by a military governor, the château is carved into a hillside laced with marl caves once used for gatherings and grand events. Today, it is best known for its culinary legacy, home to a Michelin-starred restaurant and a Bib Gourmand bistro, though its newest chapter includes seven elegantly restored suites in the 17th-century lodgment. The setting is dramatic, the history palpable, and the food delectable.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are not allowed.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Pulitzer Amsterdam in Amsterdam
ld.description: Things are a little bit different in Amsterdam. Here, for instance, Pulitzer refers to Peter, grandson of the journalism prize’s founder and obsessive fan of the town’s stately old canal houses. Putting his money where his mouth was (“the house of your neighbor is for sale only once,” he said), he set about rescuing them from ruin bit by bit; thus we have today’s Hotel Pulitzer, a five-star hotel complex comprising 25 of the photogenic 17th-century edifices along the Prinsengracht and Keizersgracht.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed on a request basis. The cost is 50 EUR per pet per day.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: The Dylan Amsterdam in Amsterdam
ld.description: Hard to believe, but there was a time when luxury hotels and boutique hotels were two distinct species. The Dylan Amsterdam, discreetly hidden away in a pair of historic buildings alongside the Keizersgracht canal, was one of the first hotels to combine boutique aesthetics with luxury comforts, and thanks to a process of continual reinvention it looks as fresh today as it did when it opened its doors in 1999.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Hotel TwentySeven Amsterdam in Amsterdam
ld.description: The first Dutch boutique hotels we saw were marvels of the modern minimalism that was in the ascendant in the turn-of-the-millennium Netherlands. Since then, however, we’ve seen a flowering of eclectic styles — but none quite so ornate as that on display in Hotel TwentySeven. This 1916 building on the central Dam Square is home to a private club for the upper crust of Amsterdam society and industry, and, on its upper floors, to a luxury boutique hotel that’s as intensely atmospheric as anything we’ve ever seen.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Van Oys Maastricht Retreat in Maastricht
ld.description: Quiet luxury might have become an overused buzz phrase, but it’s hard to find a better way to describe Van Oys Maastricht Retreat. Sophisticated guest rooms blend natural stone walls and exposed beams with muted earthy shades, and in the higher category rooms, private terraces and balconies look onto the surrounding gardens. The same soothing palette sets the scene in the spa, which eschews the latest trend for high tech treatments and anti-aging in favor of back-to-basics relaxation. But the true heart of the hotel lies in the kitchen, with farm-to-table fare at Maes and elegant fine dining at Create complemented by wine ateliers and cooking classes led by Michelin-experienced chefs for a fuller immersion in the local terroir.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed on request. Charges may apply.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Tivoli Doelen Amsterdam in Amsterdam
ld.description: It’s no small distinction, being the oldest hotel in one of the largest cities in Europe. Amsterdam was founded in the 14th century, and the 300-year-old building that’s now the Tivoli Doelen Amsterdam Doelen has had its doors open to overnight guests for a substantial part of that history. It’s true, of course, in hotels and in life, that you can’t have everything. You can’t have history and culture and location — the brick building is even older than the hotel, with an enviable address on the edge of the Kloveniersburgwal canal in the heart of the historic center — and also have huge suites with picture windows and Jacuzzi tubs.
ld.petsAllowed: Please note dogs and cats are allowed, max. weight 25kg. Limited availability, please contact the hotel before booking. A charge of 40€ per day will be applied (max. 2 pets per room). Guide dogs free of charge.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Soho House Amsterdam in Amsterdam
ld.description: The Soho House model — a members’ club oriented towards professionals in the arts and creative fields — was always destined to be a good fit for Amsterdam, not only because its intended audience is plentiful here, but also because its eclectic aesthetic is a perfect match for a city whose styles range from historic canal-house coziness to stark postmodern minimalism.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are not allowed.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

pages.h1: Pillows Grand Boutique Hotel Ter Borch Zwolle

ld.name: Pillows Grand Boutique Hotel Ter Borch Zwolle in Zwolle
ld.description: The Dutch-based Pillows Hotels chain isn’t notable just for putting its soft, plush stamp on familiar places like Amsterdam and Brussels. It’s also taking us to some of the region’s less-traveled places — like the Dutch city of Zwolle, home of Pillows Grand Boutique Hotel Ter Borch Zwolle. And while it’s clear from the exterior that this building has some history — it’s a 19th-century police station, in fact — the hotel inside is brand new. Thus classic architectural style meets contemporary design and modern comfort, a combination which, when it comes to hotels, is more or less the best of all possible worlds.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Rosewood Amsterdam in Amsterdam
ld.description: A hotel could do a lot worse, when it comes to raw material, than the old Palace of Justice, the 17th-century canal-side landmark where the Rosewood Amsterdam makes its home. The Prinsengracht location is both prominent and central, and the hotel’s designer, Piet Boon, leans into Amsterdam’s high-culture heritage, decorating its interiors with no fewer than a thousand original artworks.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Landgoed Hotel Het Roode Koper in Ermelo
ld.description: In the heart of the Veluwe forest, Het Roode Koper has been a family-run hotel since 1947, when the current owners’ grandparents opened its doors. The atmosphere is calm, with classic gardens, a pool, and direct access to the surrounding woodlands. Guests are encouraged to bring hiking boots, bikes, or a racket to make the most of the estate’s outdoor spaces. The main house is surrounded by gardens, while private villas offer a more secluded stay, including one with its own spa, just a short drive away. It is a place for resets, not rushed itineraries.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Mooirivier in Dalfsen
ld.description: The location on the banks of the Vecht is beautiful – so green and so peaceful – and it’s just as pleasant inside, with large rooms equipped with modern comforts. It’s a place which suits one and all, from businesspeople to leisure guests. The kitchen team serves up a generous take on contemporary cuisine, producing varied and delicious flavours.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are not allowed.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: The Craftsmen in Amsterdam
ld.description: Once home to the long-running Hotel Brouwer, The Craftsmen isn’t your typical canal-side stay. Housed in a 17th-century townhouse overlooking Amsterdam’s Singel, this spirited boutique hotel is where Dutch artistry takes center stage. Each of its 14 rooms honors a historic trade, from cartographers to shoemakers, all with upcycled antiques and bespoke pieces. Expect vintage tools turned into light fixtures, penny-farthings in bathrooms, and airplane doors repurposed as wardrobes. It’s wildly inventive, warmly personal, and still carries the soul of a family-run inn, albeit with a lot more imagination.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: De Plesman Hotel The Hague in The Hague
ld.description: Transforming the former headquarters of the Dutch aviation company KLM into a hotel for modern travelers feels like a fitting homage to the airline’s founder Albert Plesman. To respect the history and architectural heritage of the landmark 1930s building, many of the original design elements have been retained, including the austere brick and concrete façade, the revolving entrance door, and inside, the KLM reception desks. Also look up to spot the original ceilings near the elevators, which nod to the shape of an aircraft engine.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Villa Pétrusse in Luxembourg City
ld.description: For almost thirty years the Villa Pétrusse sat empty, its salons shuttered and gardens overgrown. Built in 1880 by textile merchant Henri-Eugène de Kerkhove, with architecture by Pierre Kemp and landscaping by Édouard André, it was once considered a “miniature château.” Its recent restoration has given the villa new life without erasing its past: worn stone staircases, hidden passages, and preserved details now stand alongside 22 rooms, suites, and a penthouse. Overlooking the Pétrusse River and Adolphe Bridge, the hotel captures both the romance of its history and the vitality of its new chapter.
ld.petsAllowed: Pets are allowed on request. Charges may apply.

award.awardFor: Two MICHELIN Keys · An exceptional stay

ld.name: Le Place d’Armes in Luxembourg City
ld.description: There’s no place quite like Luxembourg City, so it’s fitting that one of its finest hotels should be an unusual one; Hotel Le Place d’Armes is built from a string of seven 18th-century buildings, joined together right in the historic center of town. Its warrenlike interiors contain a mere 30 rooms and suites, where period architectural details like stone walls and timbered ceilings contrast with contemporary furnishings and fixtures. Along with its bundles of personality it’s got all the comforts of a much larger luxury hotel, including among its restaurants Le Cristallerie.

award.awardFor: One MICHELIN Key · A very special stay

ld.name: Schloss Eberstein in Gernsbach
ld.description: Sitting high on a peak with sweeping valley views, this historical castle is a family-owned hotel decorated with taste and style. The 16 rooms all come with attractive views of the castle courtyard or valleys, which can be explored by bike or via the various hiking trails that surround the hotel. The Schloss-Schänke restaurant serves cuisine from the Baden region and there’s an outdoor terrace and beer garden for summer, while Werners Restaurant holds One-MICHELIN-Star.

ld.name: AMERON Neuschwanstein Alpsee Resort & Spa in Schwangau
ld.description: There are few places in Europe as picturesque as this corner of Bavaria, where the fairy-tale Neuschwanstein Castle stands on a forested mountainside overlooking the waters of the Alpsee and the peaks beyond. The Ameron Neuschwanstein Alpsee Resort & Spa takes some of its stylistic cues from the ornate historicist castle, as it includes three antique hotels among its buildings; to these it adds a pair of contemporary buildings that complement the historical structures without imitating them.
ld.petsAllowed: \n Pets are allowed on request and only allowed in the Deluxe Rooms in the Galeria building at a surcharge of 25€ per night.

ld.name: Kloster Hornbach in Hornbach
ld.description: Monasteries aren’t the only ancient lodgings that are well suited for conversion into luxury hotels, but in a way, a Benedictine monastery, such as Kloster Hornbach, in the Rhineland-Palatinate, might be the most appropriate of all. The Benedictine tradition is all about hospitality, and we’re not being entirely flippant when we say the Benedictine monasteries practically invented what we now think of as extraordinary hotel service. Let everyone that comes be received as Christ, says the Rule, which today’s secular hoteliers might take to mean rolling out the red carpet for each and every guest; and the injunction to avoid lingering with guests might be the what we mean when we say that a good hotel staff is a model of discretion.

ld.name: Villa Mittermeier in Rothenburg ob der Tauber
ld.description: The Bavarian town of Rothenburg ob der Tauber is a beautifully preserved medieval gem, but that doesn’t mean its lodgings are necessarily backward-looking in their style. Villa Mittermeier stands right by the Würzburger Gate at the entrance to Rothenburg’s old town, and the building that it occupies is indeed a classic one. But what family owners Ulli and Christian Mittermeier have created here is a boutique hotel that’s right at home in the 21st century.

ld.name: Hanusel Hof in Hellengerst
ld.description: This family-run hotel with modern Alpine rooms is on the site of a former farmstead dating from 1714. By the hotel are a golf course and cross-country skiing trails. Cheerful restaurant rooms – the area towards the terrace is particularly bright.

ld.name: Strandhotel Fischland in Dierhagen
ld.description: Germany’s Baltic coast may not be balmy, but it’s pleasant all the same — all the more so with a modern, wellness-focused hotel like the Strandhotel Fischland to serve as a home base. As you might expect, it’s less focused strictly on sun and surf and more on a capacious spa and a long list of sporting activities, some indoor, some outdoor, and others on the water. The rooms are handsome and contemporary, though far from avant-garde, and the restaurants and bars range from the fine-dining Ostseelounge to the more casual Marktplatz and Spa-bistro.

ld.name: DAS.HOCHGRAT in Oberstaufen
ld.description: Das Hochgrat has mastered the contemporary alpine chalet idiom on the main drag in Oberstaufen, Germany, not far from the Swiss border. Apartment-style chalets combine clean lines and natural materials like warm wood and stone for an upscale, cozy ambience that keeps its magic even for longer stays. Roomy design kitchens, private balconies, and personal fireplaces set the tone for mountain conviviality. Just outside, the 360-degree panoramas don’t hurt, either.

ld.name: Staudacherhof in Garmisch-Partenkirchen
ld.description: The idea of a Bavarian mountain lodge might feel a bit old-fashioned, but it really shouldn’t. With winter sports — and adventure travel in general — more popular than ever, it’s a type of hospitality that’s correspondingly more relevant than ever. The fact that this part of the world’s been at it longer than most means their expertise is worth trusting. And hotels like Staudacherhof, in Garmisch-Partenkirchen, prove that the form is open to stylistic evolution and even innovation.

ld.name: Haubers Naturresort in Oberstaufen
ld.description: Please note: Some areas of Haubers Naturresort are undergoing renovations. The work is on-going and expected to be complete by the end of 2026. The hotel is taking all necessary precaustions to ensure that guest's stays are not interrupted.

ld.name: Gewandhaus Dresden in Dresden
ld.description: This smart boutique hotel has been tastefully designed with a sense of the history of the building it occupies. Stylishly designed guestrooms, from standards to junior suites. (m)eatery, its elegant restaurant, serves international fare such as dry-aged beef, steak tartare, fish and burgers. Freshly baked cakes at Kuchen Atelier (Wed-Sun).

ld.name: Spa & Resort Bachmair Weissach in Rottach-Egern
ld.description: When in Bavaria, do as the Bavarians do — no need to go full lederhosen, but a salubrious Alpine retreat by Lake Tegernsee absolutely fits the bill. Here sits Hotel Bachmair Weissach in all its renovated 19th-century glory, clearly reveling in its regional heritage: from the ornately muraled plaster façade to the sloping roofs and stout beams overhead, this is South German wholesomeness given form. Or wellness, we should say; the expansive on-site spa and fitness facilities include not just one but two spas, the more traditional Family Spa as well as the Mizu Onsen Spa, a finely crafted adaptation of the Japanese hot-spring bath that’s like nothing else in Germany.

ld.name: Aethos Monterosa in Champoluc
ld.description: Though it’s less famous than some other Alpine ski resorts, Monterosa is spectacular — and Champoluc, its largest village, is directly connected to the lift system for easy access. It’s here that you’ll find Aethos Monterosa, a hotel whose mission is to place as few obstacles as possible between you and the adventure you’ve come to the Alps to experience.

ld.name: Only YOU Hotel Atocha in Madrid
ld.description: If you’ve traveled all the way to Madrid, it might seem like an unusual decision to stay in a hotel that models itself after its counterparts in New York. But stay with us on this, because Only YOU Hotel Atocha is an inspired mix of the best of the old world and new. New York might serve as inspiration, but this hotel doesn’t ignore its heritage or its prime location in central Madrid. Catalan designer Lázaro Rosa Violan has taken a historic 19th-century building, just steps from the city’s beloved green lung, Retiro Park, and fashioned it into a 21st-century interior design gem.

ld.name: Ohla Eixample in Barcelona
ld.description: Barcelona has long been something of a hotbed of boutique-hotel style, and the original Ohla Barcelona stands out even in a crowded field. So it’s with great enthusiasm that we report that Ohla Eixample is, essentially, more of the same. The façade, with its repetitive geometric patterns, announces that this is no ordinary hotel. And what’s behind that façade is modernism of the most utopian, optimistic sort — if not for the blazing Mediterranean sun outside, you might just wonder if you were in Stockholm or Copenhagen.

ld.name: The Principal Madrid in Madrid
ld.description: The Spanish hotelier Pau Guardans believes that hotels should function as “engines of local communities,” a concept that guided the look and feel of his first two hotels — the Único in Madrid and the 1920s-style Grand Hotel Central in Barcelona. With his latest project, the Principal, he’s reinvigorated another grand old building, this one a Spanish Renaissance-style jewel located on a prominent corner of Madrid’s Gran Vía, adapting its spacious interiors for modern living.

ld.name: Little Beach House Barcelona in Garraf
ld.description: First, a word about the name. Little Beach House Barcelona is set not in Barcelona proper, but a half-hour away in Garraf, a fishing village turned holiday spot. And with 17 rooms it’s really only little when compared with the urban properties that are the core of the Soho House collection. It’s a restoration of a Fifties hotel which leaves just enough of the original intact for a bit of retro atmosphere. The rest is pure Soho House, which is to say easygoing, bohemian glamour — words that apply just as appropriately to the hotel as to its clientele.

ld.name: Yurbban Passage in Barcelona
ld.description: Between the cute modern name and the youth-oriented bells and whistles — there’s a photo booth, shuffleboard, and a juice bar called Flax & Kale Passage — it’s got all the trappings of a hotel designed for millennials. But Yurbban Passage Hotel & Spa is also rooted in Barcelona’s history: this boutique hotel is located inside a 19th-century former textile factory. And while fun in the hospitality world is sometimes posed as an alternative to luxury, here the two virtues are complementary; while the Yurbban hotels aren’t intended as top-tier luxury hotels, their comforts are substantial.

ld.name: Six Senses Ibiza in Ibiza
ld.description: The Six Senses hotels and the Balearic island of Ibiza are both so highly regarded that the conjunction of the two more or less sells itself. It’s set at the end of a peninsula in the far north of the island, a setting which maximizes its private-island atmosphere, and not only is it as luxurious as you’d rightly expect from Six Senses, but it’s extraordinarily green as well, the first BREEAM-certified resort in the region — meaning not only that its construction and operation are low-impact, but that it works with local agencies to constantly improve its environment and its surrounding communities.

ld.name: Hotel de Rome in Berlin
ld.description: It doesn’t get much heavier than the Hotel de Rome, a converted 19th-century bank building off the Bebelplatz in old East Berlin — its stone walls and neoclassical architecture are a perfect match for the contemporary luxury hotel that lies within. This hotel is set to become the lodging of choice for business-class visitors, and may well see more deals done as a hotel than it did during its tenure as the GDR’s central bank.
